newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - SingTel sees lower cable costs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - SingTel sees lower cable costs.

text.p: The cost of making long distance telephone calls will fall once a giant new submarine optic fibre cable from Asia to Europe is completed, officials at Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) said on Monday.

The general manager of SingTel's submarine cable development division, Sng Koon Pin, said the 38,000-km (23,600-mile) network, stretching from the South Pacific to the North Atlantic across Asia and the Middle East, would compete directly with satellites for intercontinental telecommunications traffic.

"Over the years, subsea cables are much cheaper. Figures are not clear, but over about a 20 year period, we think the international transmission cost of using satellites is about double (the cost of) using the new subsea cable for international calls," Sng told Reuters in an interview.

According to figures published in December by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission, the cost of international transmission represents about a third of the total cost of making an intercontinental telephone call.

SingTel was one of 86 companies which signed a US$1.3 billion agreement on January 15 to build the new network, dubbed SEA-ME-WE 3, which will be able to serve half the world's population when it is completed by the turn of the century.
The first two legs of the twin 10-gigabit network, between Europe and Singapore and from Singapore to Europe, will begin operations at the end of 1998.

The head of SingTel's international network services department Chia Choon Wei said charges to telephone users might not directly reflect the reduction in transmission costs offered by the new generation of submarine cabling.

But he said the optic fibre cables, which provide the very high quality communications needed for services such as the Internet computer network, would help contribute to the current lower trend for international phone charges.
"Eventually costs could be flattened out and not differ much based on distance...That could happen with the next generation of systems," Chia told Reuters in the interview.
He said the main advantage of the new cable network would be flexibility for telecoms operators, allowing them to use satellites or cables depending on their needs.
"Satellites are serving a different market. They are very good at broadcasting. Cables are better where high quality, high speed is needed," he said.

Sng said SingTel and its French partners, France Telecom FTE.PA, which have pioneered a series of long distance submarine cables over the last decade, had embarked on the SEA-ME-WE 3 network because its predecessor, SEA-ME-WE 2 was unable to cope with the increasing telephone traffic.
"SEA-ME-WE 2 (which can handle two times 560 megabits of data) is quite congested in certain sections. I think overall the fill-rate would be about 65-70 percent," Sng said.
"As a minimum, the SEA-ME-WE is 32 times the transmission size of SEA-ME-WE 2. Potentially 64 times if we upgrade it."
He said the new cable would have a design life of at least seven years but did not rule out discussion of yet another, even bigger, cable network before the turn of the century.
"This network will take us into the 21st century," said Chia. "We don't rule out a SEA-ME-WE 4. The question is when we start."
